blocks.content: Object-oriented programming provides two ways to reuse code: Inheritance and Composition.
1. What Inheritance and Composition Mean

["Inheritance represents an \"is-a\" relationship. For example, a Dog is an Animal.
","Composition represents a \"has-a\" relationship. For example, a Car has an Engine."]
items: Inheritance represents an "is-a" relationship. For example, a Dog is an Animal.
Composition represents a "has-a" relationship. For example, a Car has an Engine.

blocks.content: Inheritance is often the first approach developers learn because it looks simple and reduces code duplication. However, as applications grow, large inheritance hierarchies can become difficult to maintain and tightly coupled.
Composition takes a different approach. Instead of extending existing classes, a class is built by combining smaller, focused objects that each handle a specific responsibility.
Because composition creates more flexible, reusable, and loosely coupled designs, modern software development generally follows the principle:
Favor Composition Over Inheritance

In this lesson, we'll understand why inheritance can become problematic, how composition solves those problems, and why many design patterns, such as the Strategy Pattern, are built around composition.
2. What Inheritance Actually Commits You To
blocks.text: 2. What Inheritance Actually Commits You To

blocks.content: At first glance, inheritance looks like a simple way to reuse code.
When class B extends class A, the obvious benefit is that B automatically gets all the functionality of A without rewriting it.
Here, Dog can use the eat() method without implementing it again. This is the main advantage of inheritance: code reuse. However, inheritance comes with a hidden cost.
When Dog extends Animal, it becomes tightly coupled to Animal. The child class now depends on the parent's structure, behavior, and future changes.
If the parent class changes, the child class may also need to change.

Now every subclass automatically inherits sleep() whether it needs it or not. As more methods and behaviors are added to the parent, subclasses become increasingly dependent on the parent class. This creates tight coupling through inheritance.
Unlike normal coupling where one class simply calls another, inheritance creates a much stronger dependency because the child becomes part of the parent's design.
A simple way to think about it is:
With inheritance, you don't just reuse a parent's code you inherit its future changes too.

This is why inheritance can become difficult to maintain in large systems. A change in the parent class can unexpectedly impact many subclasses, making the entire hierarchy harder to understand, test, and evolve.
3. The four ways inheritance breaks down as a system grows
blocks.text: 3. The four ways inheritance breaks down as a system grows

blocks.content:
["Forced Overrides: A parent method works for most child classes, but some children need different behavior. They are forced to override the method, sometimes with empty code or an error.
","Fragile Base Class: A small change in the parent class can unexpectedly affect all child classes, causing bugs in places you didn't expect.
","Single Inheritance Limitation: A class can usually extend only one parent class. If it needs features from multiple parents, inheritance becomes difficult.
","Deep Hierarchies Are Hard to Understand: When inheritance chains become long, you must check multiple parent classes to understand how a method actually works.
"]
items: Forced Overrides: A parent method works for most child classes, but some children need different behavior. They are forced to override the method, sometimes with empty code or an error.
Fragile Base Class: A small change in the parent class can unexpectedly affect all child classes, causing bugs in places you didn't expect.
Single Inheritance Limitation: A class can usually extend only one parent class. If it needs features from multiple parents, inheritance becomes difficult.
Deep Hierarchies Are Hard to Understand: When inheritance chains become long, you must check multiple parent classes to understand how a method actually works.

blocks.content: In short: Inheritance can lead to forced changes, unexpected bugs, design limitations, and code that's harder to understand.
4. What Composition Does Differently
Composition takes a different approach to code reuse.

Instead of creating an "is-a" relationship through inheritance, composition creates a "has-a" relationship. Rather than inheriting behavior from a parent class, a class contains other objects and delegates work to them.
For example, instead of making a Penguin a special type of Bird that inherits a fly() method it cannot use, we can separate the movement behavior into its own class.
Now a bird simply has a movement behavior.
Different birds can use different movement behaviors.
Notice that no inheritance hierarchy is needed.
The Bird class does not know whether it is flying or swimming. It simply delegates that responsibility to the object it contains.
This is the key idea behind composition:
Instead of inheriting behavior, a class is built by combining smaller, reusable objects.
Because these objects are independent, they can be changed, replaced, or extended without modifying the main class.
This makes composition more flexible, easier to maintain, and far less coupled than inheritance.
5. Bird Problem: Inheritance vs Composition
Watch what happens to the Penguin class specifically. In the inheritance version, it inherits something it has to actively reject.
In the composition version, it simply never receives a behavior it doesn't have there's nothing to override, because nothing was forced on it in the first place.
INHERITANCE: Penguin is forced to override a method it can't honor
COMPOSITION: each class holds exactly the behavior it actually has
6. Behavior Swapping at Runtime
Inheritance fixes a class's behavior at compile time once Penguin extends Bird is written, that relationship is permanent for every Penguin object that will ever exist.

Composition holds the behavior as a regular field, which means it can be swapped out after the object already exists, while the program is running. This single property is the foundation of the strategy pattern, the most common practical use of composition.
This pattern define a family of interchangeable behaviors behind one interface, hold one of them as a composed field, and allow swapping which one is held is formally known as the strategy pattern.

It's the textbook demonstration of why composition is more flexible: inheritance can never do this, because which class you extend is decided once, at compile time, and cannot change for the lifetime of an object.
7. When Inheritance Is Still the Right
blocks.text: 7. When Inheritance Is Still the Right

blocks.content: The principle "Favor Composition Over Inheritance" does not mean inheritance is bad or should never be used.
Instead, it means that composition should be your default choice, and inheritance should be used only when there is a true and stable is-a relationship.
A good inheritance relationship exists when the subclass is genuinely a more specific version of the parent in every meaningful way, and that relationship is unlikely to change in the future.

For example, a Savings Account is a type of Bank Account. Every Savings Account shares the core characteristics of a Bank Account while adding some specialized behavior. The relationship is natural, easy to understand, and remains valid throughout the lifetime of the system.
Inheritance works well when:

["The relationship is truly is-a, not just a way to reuse code.","All subclasses can honor the behavior and contract of the parent class.","The hierarchy is stable and unlikely to change frequently.","The parent provides behavior that is genuinely shared by all subclasses."]
items: The relationship is truly is-a, not just a way to reuse code.
All subclasses can honor the behavior and contract of the parent class.
The hierarchy is stable and unlikely to change frequently.
The parent provides behavior that is genuinely shared by all subclasses.

blocks.content: The mistake many developers make is using inheritance simply because they want to reuse a few methods. Code reuse alone is usually not a strong enough reason to create an inheritance hierarchy.
A useful rule of thumb is:
Use inheritance when the relationship is naturally and permanently "is-a." Use composition when you simply want to reuse behavior.

In modern software design, inheritance is still valuable, but it should be used carefully and intentionally. When there is any doubt about whether the relationship is truly an "is-a" relationship, composition is usually the safer and more flexible choice.
8. When to Use Inheritance vs Composition
blocks.text: 8. When to Use Inheritance vs Composition

blocks.content: There is no rule that says inheritance is always wrong or composition is always right. The key is understanding the problem you are trying to solve.
1. Inheritance Is a Good Fit When
blocks.text: 1. Inheritance Is a Good Fit When

blocks.content: Inheritance works best when there is a genuine and permanent is-a relationship between the parent and child classes.
Use inheritance when:

["Every subclass is truly a more specific version of the parent.","All subclasses should share the same interface and behavior contract.","The hierarchy is simple and shallow, usually one or two levels deep.","The behavior is fixed and does not need to change after the object is created."]
items: Every subclass is truly a more specific version of the parent.
All subclasses should share the same interface and behavior contract.
The hierarchy is simple and shallow, usually one or two levels deep.
The behavior is fixed and does not need to change after the object is created.

blocks.content: In these situations, inheritance provides a natural and clean way to model the relationship.
2. Composition Is a Good Fit When
blocks.text: 2. Composition Is a Good Fit When

blocks.content: Composition works best when behavior should be assembled from independent pieces rather than inherited from a parent.
Use composition when:

["Different objects need different combinations of behavior.","Behavior may need to change after an object has been created.","Multiple capabilities need to be combined without forcing them into a single inheritance hierarchy.","Individual behaviors should be tested independently and reused across multiple classes."]
items: Different objects need different combinations of behavior.
Behavior may need to change after an object has been created.
Multiple capabilities need to be combined without forcing them into a single inheritance hierarchy.
Individual behaviors should be tested independently and reused across multiple classes.

blocks.content: Composition focuses on flexibility by building objects from smaller reusable components.

Note

Rule of Thumb

A simple rule to remember is:

- If the relationship is truly and permanently "is-a", use inheritance.

- If you are mainly trying to reuse, combine, or swap behavior, use composition.

In modern software design, composition is usually the safer default because it creates more flexible, maintainable, and loosely coupled systems.

blocks.content: 9. Common Mistakes

["Mistake 1: Using inheritance only for code reuse: Don't use inheritance just because the parent class has useful code. If the child is not really a type of the parent, use composition instead.
","Mistake 2: Creating too many subclasses: Making a new subclass for every behavior combination quickly becomes difficult to manage. Composition lets you combine behaviors without creating many classes.
","Mistake 3: Overriding methods to do nothing: If a subclass overrides a method with an empty body or throws an exception, the inheritance relationship is probably wrong.
","Mistake 4: Never using inheritance: Composition is usually preferred, but inheritance is still useful when there is a clear and permanent is-a relationship.
"]
items: Mistake 1: Using inheritance only for code reuse: Don't use inheritance just because the parent class has useful code. If the child is not really a type of the parent, use composition instead.

Mistake 2: Creating too many subclasses: Making a new subclass for every behavior combination quickly becomes difficult to manage. Composition lets you combine behaviors without creating many classes.
Mistake 3: Overriding methods to do nothing: If a subclass overrides a method with an empty body or throws an exception, the inheritance relationship is probably wrong.
Mistake 4: Never using inheritance: Composition is usually preferred, but inheritance is still useful when there is a clear and permanent is-a relationship.

blocks.content: 10. Quick Reference
Inheritance: Inheritance represents an is-a relationship where a child class extends a parent class.
Composition: Composition represents a has-a relationship where a class uses other objects to get behavior.
Fragile Base Class Problem: A change in the parent class can unexpectedly affect all subclasses.
Runtime Flexibility: Composition allows behavior to be changed while the application is running.
Strategy Pattern: The Strategy Pattern uses composition to switch between different behaviors easily.
General Rule: Favor composition by default and use inheritance only for a true is-a relationship.
